records.sourceFile: Concussion symptoms among athletes - Preinjury factors predict postinjury factors.pdf

paper.citation: Sinnott AM, Kontos AP, Collins MW, Ortega J. Concussion Symptoms Among Athletes: Preinjury Factors Predict Postinjury Factors. Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation. 2020;35(4):E361-E371.
paper.abstract: This retrospective analysis of 290 high school and collegiate-aged athletes tested whether preinjury Post-Concussion Symptom Scale factors predict postinjury symptom factors. In the combined sample, preinjury cognitive-sensory symptoms and female sex predicted cognitive-migraine-fatigue symptoms, and in age-specific models preinjury sleep-arousal symptoms predicted somatic and sleep factors in 14 to 17 year olds, while preinjury affective symptoms predicted affective and somatic factors in 18 to 21 year olds. The authors conclude that symptom factors may help clinicians interpret symptom clusters, particularly in adolescents.
paper.tldr: Symptoms reported before the season predicted some post-concussion symptom patterns, and the pattern differed between high school and college-aged athletes. The study is retrospective and explains a modest share of the variation, so it supports better symptom interpretation rather than individual prognosis.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of the 22-item Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) embedded in ImPACT testing from a community surveillance programme in northern California (2008 to 2017). Preinjury and postinjury PCSS scores were grouped into four preinjury and four postinjury symptom factors from a previously published factor structure, and linear regressions tested whether preinjury factors, sex and prior concussion predicted postinjury factors in 14 to 17 and 18 to 21 year olds and combined, with a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of .0083.
paper.findings: Of 772 subjects, 290 were analysed (mean age 16.99 years). In the combined sample, preinjury cognitive-sensory symptoms (P = .002) and female sex (P = .002) predicted the postinjury cognitive-migraine-fatigue factor, and prior concussion predicted the somatic factor (P = .005). In 14 to 17 year olds, preinjury sleep-arousal predicted postinjury somatic (P = .003) and sleep (P = .005) factors. In 18 to 21 year olds, preinjury affective symptoms predicted postinjury affective (P = .001) and somatic (P = .009) factors. Postinjury assessment took place on average 3 days after injury.
paper.limitations: The design is retrospective, the analysis used raw PCSS scores rather than change scores, and lifestyle factors such as activity, sleep and medication were not controlled. The authors did not assess honesty or effort in symptom reporting, and did not record race, ethnicity, language or multisport status. The paper has internal inconsistencies: Methods exclude evaluations more than 8 days after injury but Results say 7; the 18 to 21 year old somatic result is P = .008 in the abstract and P = .009 in the Results, which is above the stated corrected alpha of .0083; and the Discussion and Conclusion describe predictions (cognitive-sensory for both age groups, affective to sleep in 18 to 21 year olds) that Table 5 does not show.
paper.practicalImplications: When an athlete reports sleep or emotional symptoms before the season, clinicians can ask more detailed questions about onset and daily course, since these preseason patterns were linked to specific post-injury symptom groups. The paper gives no validated prognostic score, so the findings should prompt questions rather than set expected recovery.
paper.athleteDev: For performance and wellbeing staff, preseason reports of sleep or mood complaints may flag athletes whose post-injury symptom profile needs closer watch. The paper does not assess training or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The paper does not give return-to-play criteria or timing. Its finding that preseason symptom patterns relate to post-injury symptom profiles may help decide who needs closer symptom tracking after injury, but it should not be used to decide when an athlete can return to play.

records.sourceFile: Considering the effects of cannabinoids and exercise on the brain - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Rajaei AY, Neary JP, Thompson ES, Singh J, Mang CS. Considering the Effects of Cannabinoids and Exercise on the Brain: A Narrative Review. Sports. 2025;13:320.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes overlapping effects of cannabinoids and exercise on brain function through inflammation, vascular function and neuroplasticity, with attention to athletes. The authors conclude that combined effects could be additive, synergistic or opposing, and that direct study of the interaction is scarce.
paper.tldr: A mechanistic review suggesting that cannabinoids and exercise act on shared brain-relevant pathways, with THC and CBD producing different effects. The combined effects in athletes have not been tested directly.
paper.methods: Narrative review. The authors searched PubMed and Google Scholar with combined keywords, emphasizing work from 2010 onward, and two authors screened titles and abstracts. They included 243 references, judging quality informally by journal credibility and the alignment of methods, results and conclusions, with no systematic protocol, inclusion criteria or formal appraisal tool.
paper.findings: The authors report that exercise and the endocannabinoid system both influence inflammation, cerebral blood flow and neuroplasticity. In the cited work, single bouts of treadmill running or cycling raised circulating anandamide, and THC-dominant cannabis use is described as disrupting neuroplasticity. In athletes, one cited trial reported that acute CBD improved peak oxygen consumption and lactate accumulation in endurance-trained men, and a cited female athlete study reported lower anaerobic performance in cannabis users.
paper.limitations: Narrative design with a non-systematic search and no formal quality appraisal. Most mechanistic evidence comes from animal, cell and non-athlete studies, and the authors state that few human or athlete studies have tested cannabinoid-exercise interaction. The concussion and pain applications are described as largely unstudied.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should treat cannabinoid use in athletes as an unresolved question. The review gives no dosing, safety or return-to-play guidance, and its authors call for direct study before therapeutic use.
paper.athleteDev: The review reports no performance outcomes. Staff can note the authors' view that habitual exercise might offset some effects of THC-dominant cannabis on neuroplasticity, but this is speculative and untested.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return to sport. Concussion and pain are discussed only as speculative targets, and the only post-concussion cannabinoid evidence cited is a single small report in females with post-concussion syndrome.

paper.citation: Roschel H, Gualano B, Ostojic SM, Rawson ES. Creatine Supplementation and Brain Health. Nutrients. 2021;13:586.
paper.abstract: This short review updates evidence on creatine supplementation and brain health in humans. Creatine may improve cognitive processing, especially where brain creatine is low because of acute stressors such as exercise or sleep deprivation, or chronic conditions. The optimal protocol to raise brain creatine has not been established, and studies that measure brain creatine and cognition together are needed.
paper.tldr: Creatine may help cognition when the brain is stressed, such as during sleep loss or hypoxia, but the dose and duration needed to raise brain creatine are not settled. Human evidence for concussion recovery is limited, so the authors describe high-risk use as a judgment rather than a proven treatment.
paper.methods: Narrative review of human and animal studies on brain creatine, cognition and brain injury. No systematic search method is described. The authors summarize study protocols and outcomes in a table of cognitive studies and discuss findings on brain creatine uptake, sleep deprivation, mental fatigue, and mild traumatic brain injury.
paper.findings: The authors report that of 12 studies of creatine and brain creatine or phosphocreatine, nine showed significant increases of about 5 to 10 percent, smaller than the muscle response. Cognitive results were mixed across studies, with clearer effects under stress such as hypoxia and sleep deprivation. In children with mild traumatic brain injury, creatine was associated with improvements in several symptoms, and the authors note that the mechanistic and animal evidence is much larger than the human evidence.
paper.limitations: Studies differ in brain creatine measurement, dose, duration and population, which prevents direct comparison. The review has no described search, many cited trials did not measure brain creatine, and the authors state that human brain creatine rises only about 10 percent, which limits extrapolation from animal findings. Several authors have declared financial ties to creatine manufacturers.
paper.practicalImplications: Creatine should not be presented to athletes as a proven way to protect the brain or speed concussion recovery. The authors argue that, given creatine's safety record, encouraging supplementation in populations at high risk of mild traumatic brain injury might be prudent, but they acknowledge this rests mainly on animal and theoretical data rather than clinical trials.
paper.athleteDev: The review cites studies in which creatine reduced the effect of sleep deprivation on rugby passing accuracy and improved selected cognitive indexes in semi-professional mountain bikers, while two studies in non-stressed soccer players found no effect on passing accuracy. None of these studies measured brain creatine, and the authors say transfer to sport performance remains to be shown.
paper.rtp: Not suitable for return-to-sport decisions after concussion. The authors describe the human mild traumatic brain injury evidence as scarce, with much of it from animal models, and they say it is difficult to generalize that evidence to athletes.

records.sourceFile: Does increased core temperature alter cognitive performance during exercise-induced heat strain - A narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Doohan MA, Watzek JT, King N, White MJ, Stewart IB. Does increased core temperature alter cognitive performance during exercise-induced heat strain? A narrative review. J Appl Physiol. 2023;135:35-52.
paper.abstract: Thirty-one studies that measured cognitive performance and core temperature during exercise in heat were reviewed and grouped into inhibition, working memory and cognitive flexibility tasks. Core temperature change alone did not predict cognitive performance, and effects were more likely when heat strain was combined with dehydration, prolonged exercise or high core temperatures.
paper.tldr: Heat-induced changes in core temperature alone were not a consistent predictor of cognitive decline during exercise. Impairments were more likely when heat was combined with dehydration, long exercise bouts or core temperatures near 39 C.
paper.methods: Systematic search of CINAHL, Embase and PubMed (final search 11 May 2022) for adult human studies with control and experimental conditions that measured cognitive performance and core temperature during exercise-induced heat strain. Two reviewers screened studies, and 31 studies were included in the narrative review. Hedges' g was calculated for each cognitive task at the time point with the peak core temperature difference between conditions, and risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool.
paper.findings: Core temperature changes of 0 to 1.0 C (18 studies), 1.0 to 2.0 C (7 studies) and greater than 2.0 C (2 studies) were used. The authors report that changes above 1 C were needed to influence cognitive performance across all three domains. Accuracy was more affected than response time, and reaction time, memory recall and Stroop tasks were most likely to detect change. The greatest decrements typically occurred near 39 C.
paper.limitations: Small samples (mean 16 participants per study), a modest number of studies with usable data (four of 31 could not have peak core temperature changes identified because data were not shared), and differing protocols and task designs. The authors judged a meta-analysis inappropriate for these reasons. All studies had a moderate overall risk of bias.
paper.practicalImplications: When heat strain is a concern, staff should consider hydration status, exercise duration and core temperature together, not core temperature alone, when interpreting cognitive performance. Reaction time, memory recall and Stroop tasks are the measures the authors identify as most likely to detect change.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: when testing decision-making or cognitive tasks in hot training or competition, record core temperature, hydration and exercise duration alongside the cognitive result. A small change in core temperature alone may not explain a change in performance.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It studied healthy participants in exercise heat and does not address concussion, injury or medical clearance.

records.sourceFile: Does mental fatigue negatively affect outcomes of functional performance tests.pdf

paper.citation: Verschueren J, Tassignon B, Proost M, Teugels A, Van Cutsem J, Roelands B, et al. Does Mental Fatigue Negatively Affect Outcomes of Functional Performance Tests? Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020.
paper.abstract: In 14 healthy adults, a 90-minute incongruent Stroop task increased subjective mental fatigue, and accuracy on the neurocognitive Reactive Balance Test fell after the task. Single-leg hop, countermovement jump and Y-Balance test results were not affected by mental fatigue.
paper.tldr: A 90-minute mentally demanding task reduced accuracy on a reactive balance test, while traditional strength and balance tests were unchanged. Mental fatigue may affect adaptability and decision-making in ways standard functional tests do not capture.
paper.methods: Randomized counterbalanced crossover design with 14 healthy adults. A 90-minute 100% incongruent Stroop task (mental fatigue) and a 90-minute documentary (control) were each followed by pre and post testing of single-leg hop, countermovement jump, Y-Balance test and the Reactive Balance Test (accuracy and visuomotor reaction time). Analysis used repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests.
paper.findings: Subjective mental fatigue was higher after the Stroop task than after the control task (interaction p = 0.002). Reactive Balance Test accuracy was 86.16 +/- 1.22% post mental fatigue versus 91.62 +/- 1.56% post control, with a condition by time interaction (p = 0.023 in the results text; the abstract reports p = 0.024). No condition by time interaction was found for the single-leg hop, countermovement jump, Y-Balance test, or Reactive Balance Test reaction time; small condition effects favoured the control session for single-leg hop and countermovement jump. Stroop task accuracy and reaction time did not change over the 90 minutes.
paper.limitations: Small sample of 14 healthy adults (four women), tested in a laboratory with one session per condition. No neurophysiological measures were taken. The Stroop task did not produce a behavioural decline, and the authors state that clinical applicability cannot be inferred from these first results. The abstract and results text give slightly different p-values for the Reactive Balance Test interaction (0.024 and 0.023).
paper.practicalImplications: Where decision-making and reactive balance matter, staff may consider adding a reactive or neurocognitive test to standard functional tests when an athlete is mentally fatigued. Traditional single-leg hop, countermovement jump and Y-Balance results were not changed in this study, so they should not be read as detecting mental fatigue.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: in healthy active adults, a 90-minute mentally demanding task lowered reactive balance accuracy but not jump, hop or Y-Balance results. If staff want to detect effects of mental fatigue, these data suggest reactive or decision-based tests are more sensitive than traditional jump and balance tests, though this has not been tested in athletes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It used healthy adults, no injured participants, and no return-to-play outcome, and the authors state that the clinical use of neurocognitive tests is not yet established.
